extracted.intended_audience: literate general readers of The Spectator; essayists and commentators on manners and character
extracted.subtask_description: Short essays and moral reflections that portray characters and social types by observing outward appearance, anecdotes, classical allusions, and letters; includes guidance on scope (covering all ranks) and rhetorical techniques. Geared to writing persuasive, witty periodical essays on manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form character from the 'air' of the whole face
rubrics_metrics.description: The Air of the whole Face is much more expressive than the Lines of it: The Air is generally nothing else but the inward Disposition of the Mind made visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting or judging a person, emphasize the overall 'air' or expression rather than isolated features; the face's general demeanour communicates temper and disposition more reliably than particular lines or features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physiognomy cautiously — avoid prejudiced judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: A wise Man should be particularly cautious how he gives credit to a Man's outward Appearance. It is an irreparable Injustice we are guilty of towards one another, when we are prejudiced by the Looks and Features of those whom we do not know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While immediate impressions from looks are natural and useful for characterization, writers (and readers) should guard against letting appearances dictate final moral judgments; allow narrative or philosophical reflection to show when looks deceive (e.g., Socrates resembling Silenus yet being virtuous).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground physiognomic claims with examples and authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who have established Physiognomy into an Art...have regarded the Features much more than the Air. I have seen a very ingenious Author on this Subject... Accordingly he gives the Prints of several Faces that are of a different Mould.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advancing claims about character from looks, support them with concrete examples, printed likenesses, classical references, or stories (e.g., Prince of Condé, Socrates) to give weight and illustration to the speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anecdote and exemplum to humanize and test theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates' disciples carried a physiognomist to him to put the artist to the trial...The Physiognomist pronounced him the most lewd...Socrates told them...he had conquered the strong Dispositions he was born with by the Dictates of Philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce short narratives or amusing tests of an idea (anecdotes, trials of arts) to demonstrate limitations or surprises of general principles and to engage readers through story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover all social ranks — do not omit 'inferior' circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Considerations of Mankind, as a SPECTATOR, you should not omit Circumstances which relate to the inferior Part of the World, any more than those which concern the greater. There is one thing...the general Corruption of Manners in the Servants of Great Britain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodical essays should address behaviours across social strata (including servants, grooms, lacqueys) — treating everyday, lower-status scenes (coffee-houses, alehouses, parks) yields material for social satire and comprehensive moral observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use social examples to expose public vices and correct manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The Complaint...runs wholly upon Men-Servants...I can attribute the Licentiousness...to the Custom of giving Board-Wages...it makes them...assume in a humourous Way the Names and Titles of those whose Liveries they wear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To criticize or reform social ills, trace concrete institutional or habitual causes (e.g., board-wages, habits of servants), give vivid scenes (Hide-Park, courts of justice), and show practical consequences (robberies, insolence) so readers see the linkage of cause and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue by clear, practical considerations to persuade behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: To banish an Evil...I shall endeavour to shew the Folly of Demurrage from two or three Reflections...First...the Shortness of their Time. Second...that of Beauty is much shorter. A third...the great Danger of her falling in Love when she is about Threescore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advising or reproving (e.g., coquettes/demurrers), present a small number of strong, concrete considerations (time, transience of beauty, future risks) rather than diffuse moralizing; this focused structure persuades and is memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance moral severity with levity and illustrative stories
rubrics_metrics.description: That I may a little alleviate the Severity of this my Speculation...I shall translate a Story...The Reader will see it is not foreign to my present Subject, and I dare say will think it a lively Representation...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterbalance stern philosophical or moral claims with humorous or titillating anecdotes (e.g., Pontignan's swaddling story) to keep readers engaged and to provide relief from didacticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enrich essays with classical and poetic quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations from Ovid, Martial, Virgil, Milton, and other authorities are interspersed throughout the papers to illustrate and ornament the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ classical allusions and poetic excerpts to lend authority, elegance, and associative resonance to the essay; use them to amplify themes (beauty, time, vice) and to situate modern observations within a literary tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use letters and fictional correspondents as rhetorical devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of my Speculations...the following Letters of my Correspondents...After I have assured you I am...one of the Handsomest young Girls about Town...I now propose my self as a Foil to the Club.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame social critique by publishing (real or fictive) letters from correspondents to present diverse voices, comic extremes, or illustrative cases; letters allow dramatization of social types and supply ready-made examples for commentary.
